hero.name: Lalit
hero.who: a junior architect in Ahmedabad who freezes in every tough money conversation

story.b: Lalit gets a message from his landlord on a Sunday morning. From next month, the rent for his one-room flat in Navrangpura will go up by twenty percent. Lalit's stomach drops. He types a reply asking for less, deletes it, types again, and finally sends okay uncle, no problem. The same week, he gathers the courage to ask his manager at the architecture firm about a raise. She says the budget is very tight this year. Lalit nods, says he understands, and walks back to his desk feeling stupid. On the bus home along Ashram Road, he wonders why he can design a whole building but cannot hold one tough conversation.

ask.q: Lalit keeps giving in the moment money talks get tense. What is the most useful thing for him to learn?
o: Prepare stronger facts and arguments to win the debate
Avoid these talks, since pushing back might damage relationships
Understand and calm the other side's feelings before pushing his own point
ask.why: Tense talks are run by emotion, so facts alone often bounce off a defensive person. Showing he understands their side lowers their guard and makes room for real discussion. Avoiding the talks keeps him paying more and earning less, and the relationships do not improve either.

chapters.take: In tense talks, feelings run the room. Deal with them first.

story.b: At a housing site in Bopal, the contractor, Bhavesh, is shouting. The firm's payment is three weeks late, and he is threatening to pull his workers off tomorrow. Lalit's senior has sent him to handle it. His first instinct is to explain the firm's billing cycle. Instead, he takes a breath and speaks to what Bhavesh might be feeling. He says it sounds like Bhavesh has been paying his workers from his own pocket, and that must be stressful. Bhavesh stops mid-sentence. Then he sits down on a cement bag and says yes, for two weeks now. They talk for twenty minutes. By the end, Bhavesh agrees to continue while Lalit pushes accounts for a date.

ask.q: A furious client calls Lalit about a leaking terrace in his new house. What should Lalit say first?
o: Explain that the leak is the builder's fault, not the firm's
Name what the client must be feeling, like worry about damage to his home
Promise to fix everything today, just to end the call
ask.why: An upset person cannot hear explanations until they feel understood. Naming his worry shows Lalit gets it, which lowers his guard. Blaming the builder sounds defensive even if true, and promising what he cannot deliver will make things worse tomorrow.

chapters.take: Show people you understand their side before you argue yours.

story.b: Mrs Parikh, a retired professor, is building a bungalow, and she has just seen Lalit's second design. She frowns and says it just feels wrong. The old Lalit would rush to defend the plan, room by room. This time he simply repeats her last words gently, as a question. Feels wrong? She hesitates, then explains that the drawing room faces the road, and she likes quiet mornings. He waits. She adds that her husband passed away last year, and she spends most of her time alone. Lalit says it seems the house needs to feel calm and private more than grand. Her face softens, and she starts describing the garden she wants.

ask.q: A colleague tells Lalit the new site schedule is a disaster, then goes quiet. What is the best way to respond?
o: Gently repeat a disaster as a question, then listen and name the worry he hears
List all the reasons the schedule is actually fine
Change the subject to avoid an argument
ask.why: A gentle mirror invites the colleague to keep talking, and naming his worry shows he has been heard. That is how Lalit learns what the real problem is. Defending the schedule shuts him down before the problem comes out, and changing the subject leaves it to grow.

chapters.take: Repeat a few key words and name the feeling. Then listen.

story.h: A second try with his manager
story.b: Three months later, Lalit tries the raise conversation again. Last time he asked a yes or no question and got a no. This time he arrives with open questions. When his manager, Nandini, again says the budget is tight, he does not argue. He asks what the firm would need to see from him over the next six months for a raise to make sense. She thinks, then lists two things: handling one client project on his own, and learning the new modelling software. He asks how they could check his progress together. She suggests a review in October. Walking out, Lalit realises he now has a clear path instead of a closed door.

ask.q: A tile supplier quotes far above Lalit's project budget. Which response is most likely to move things forward?
o: Tell him flatly that the price is too high
Accept the quote to keep the relationship smooth
Ask how they could make this order work within the budget he has
ask.why: An open question invites the supplier to help solve the problem, perhaps with a different finish or a bulk discount. A flat no often makes the other side defensive, and accepting the price costs the project money it does not have. How and what questions turn opponents into problem solvers.

chapters.take: Ask how and what questions, and let the other side help solve your problem.

story.b: Lalit's rental agreement comes up for renewal in July, and his landlord, Mr Desai, hints at another increase. This time Lalit plans his words carefully. Instead of pushing for a yes, he asks something easy to say no to. Is it unfair of him to ask for the same rent if he signs for two years and handles small repairs himself? Mr Desai, a retired bank officer, visibly relaxes. He says no, it is not unfair at all, though he would want a small increase. They talk properly for the first time, over tea on the balcony. They settle on a five percent rise, a two-year agreement, and Lalit fixing the leaking tap himself.

ask.q: Lalit wants his busy senior to review his drawings this week. Which request is most likely to work?
o: Tell him firmly that he must review them by tomorrow
Ask whether it would be a bother to look at five drawings for ten minutes on Friday
Keep pleading until he finally agrees to say yes
ask.why: A question that is easy to refuse lets his senior feel safe and in control, so he is more likely to engage. A demand creates resistance, and pleading for a yes puts pressure on him, which tends to make people defensive. A relaxed no often opens the real conversation.

chapters.take: Questions that are easy to refuse make people feel safe enough to say yes.

story.h: Telling Mrs Parikh about the delay
story.b: Heavy rain and a slow approval mean Mrs Parikh's bungalow will be six weeks late. Lalit dreads telling her, because she has rented a flat only until October. Before the meeting, he writes down every harsh thing she might think about him and the firm. Careless. Bad planners. Not to be trusted. Then, at her dining table, he says them first. He says she probably feels the firm did not plan properly, and may be wondering whether their dates mean anything. Mrs Parikh blinks. Then she says she knows the rain was not his fault, and asks how she can help speed up the approval. Lalit expected anger, but found a partner.

ask.q: Lalit's friend must tell his team that weekend work is needed all this month. How should he open?
o: Name the team's likely complaints first, like feeling their weekends are not respected
Announce it quickly and move on before anyone objects
Bury the news inside a long list of good updates
ask.why: Saying the other side's fears out loud takes the sting out of them, and people often respond more gently. Rushing past it leaves the resentment unspoken and growing. Hiding bad news among good updates feels sneaky once noticed, which damages trust more than the news itself.

chapters.take: Say their worst fears about you out loud, before they do.

story.b: By October, the bungalow is nearly finished, and Mrs Parikh has recommended Lalit to two friends. Bhavesh, the contractor, now calls Lalit first when something goes wrong, before he shouts at anyone. At his review, Lalit shows Nandini the client project he handled alone and the models he built in the new software. He gets the raise, smaller than he hoped but real, and a clear plan for the next one. His rent rose only five percent. Lalit's stomach still tightens before tough talks. But now he walks in curious about the other side's feelings, instead of afraid of them. Some Sundays he still has tea with Mr Desai on the balcony.

chapters.take: Tough talks go better when you listen for feelings before you argue.
